prompt: You are shopping for your first motorcycle helmet. What should matter most?
choices: Whether its color matches your motorcycle
Finding the lowest price you can
How light it feels when you carry it
How well it protects your head in a crash
explanation: Protection comes first. Choose a helmet that meets U.S. DOT standards, fits snugly all the way around and has no defects; full-face and three-quarter styles protect best. A bright color can help others see you, but it never replaces protection.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 5 (Helmet Selection); South Carolina Motorcycle and Moped Operator Manual, p. 29

prompt: In a work zone, your lane has been grooved for repaving. How should you ride across it?
choices: Keep your eyes up, go slow and don't fight the bars
Look down at the grooves right ahead of your front tire
Brake firmly and weave to find the smoothest spots
Speed up so your tires skim across the grooves
explanation: Grooved or scored pavement can make the motorcycle wander. Keep your head and eyes up, ride slowly with a steady throttle and let the bike move a little instead of fighting the handlebars. Looking down, weaving or braking hard makes control harder.
ref: South Carolina Motorcycle and Moped Operator Manual, p. 75 (Work Zones); MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 31 (Grooves and Gratings)

prompt: Where should your passenger look as you ride through a curve?
choices: Straight down at the road beside the motorcycle
Back over their shoulder to watch traffic behind you
Over your shoulder, in the direction of the curve
Toward the outside edge of the curve
explanation: Tell passengers to stay directly behind you and look over your shoulder in the direction of turns and curves. This helps them lean with you. Turning around or looking away from the turn can upset your balance.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 35 (Preparing Your Passenger to Ride); South Carolina Motorcycle and Moped Operator Manual, p. 82

prompt: How does a three-wheel motorcycle's stability compare with a two-wheeler's?
choices: So stable that it cannot tip, since all wheels stay down
More stable, but it can lift a wheel or tip in a turn
Less stable, so it must be leaned into every turn
About the same, and it is steered the same way
explanation: With three wheels on the ground, a three-wheel motorcycle is naturally more stable. But in turns and tight maneuvers its weight can shift past its tip-over lines, lifting a wheel and possibly tipping it over. It cannot lean or countersteer; you point the front wheel where you want to go.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 49 (Three-Wheel Supplement: Steering & Tip); South Carolina Motorcycle and Moped Operator Manual, p. 93

prompt: You are about to make a turn on a three-wheel motorcycle. How should you approach it?
choices: Hold your speed and watch the road just past the front wheel
Enter at speed, then brake hard once you are in the turn
Press the inside handgrip forward to countersteer into it
Slow down first, keep your head up and look through it
explanation: Approach the turn with your head up, looking through it, and set your speed before you enter: roll off the throttle and brake to a safe speed, then release the brakes. Braking hard in the turn can cause a skid, and a three-wheeler cannot be countersteered.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, pp. 49-50 (Three-Wheel Supplement: Turning); South Carolina Motorcycle and Moped Operator Manual, p. 97

prompt: A tire suddenly goes flat while you are riding. What should you do first?
choices: Grip firmly, ease off the throttle and ride straight
Brake hard right away, using both brakes fully
Swerve onto the shoulder right away to get out of traffic
Downshift quickly so the engine slows you down
explanation: Hold the handgrips firmly, ease off the throttle and keep a straight course. If you must brake, gradually apply the brake on the tire that isn't flat (if you're sure which one), then edge to the side of the road, squeeze the clutch and stop.
ref: MSF Motorcycle Operator Manual, p. 32 (Tire Failure); South Carolina Motorcycle and Moped Operator Manual, p. 76
